item.title: As midterms loom, Justice Department keeps taking aim at Trump foes
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Attorney General Todd Blanche has been busy. In the run up to the Nov. 3 midterm elections, the nation's most powerful law enforcement official has hit the campaign trail, stumping at the Republican convention in Texas and at rallies for candidates aligned with President Donald Trump in New York and North Carolina. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. The Justice Department, under Blanche's leadership, has filed broad and controversial election-related lawsuits, including suing the state of Alaska last week to preemptively block certification of the results of the state's tight Senate race if the Republican candidate loses. The Justice Department has also executed search warrants and filed criminal charges against some of Trump's political foes, delivering on promises to the president's conservative base that current and former officials viewed as corrupt or undermining the president would face legal consequences. The Justice Department has traditionally stayed quiet in the months before an election, fearful of being perceived of using its law enforcement weight to influence elections. But Blanche has had some of his busiest weeks as attorney general ahead of next week's midterms, cannonballing into politically fraught cases as the president cheers him on. The agency's recent targets include James B. Comey, a former director of the FBI and staunch Trump critic who this month was hit with a third federal case in 13 months. The Justice Department also this week tried and failed to indict Cassidy Hutchinson, a former Trump aide, for allegedly lying to Congress during her testimony about the president's actions during the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol. Days earlier, the agency charged two former FBI officials, who have long been targets of right-wing attacks, with lying to Congress. Trump's most ardent supporters have applauded Blanche, saying the Justice Department has long been weaponized against the president and that he is bringing legitimate cases against people who they believe broke the law. "This Department is following the facts and the law, not anybody's political time table," the department said in a statement. But critics and former Justice Department attorneys say the attorney general is allowing the agency to bring weak cases aimed at seemingly delivering on the president's desire for vengeance, rather than for legitimate law enforcement reasons, before voters head to the polls. "What we're seeing at the Justice Department is deeply troubling, not because of any one case, but because of the cumulative pattern," said Perry Carbone, a longtime federal prosecutor in the Southern District of New York who left the department last year. "A Justice Department cannot maintain public trust if its decisions appear to depend on whom the president likes, whom he dislikes, or whom he wants to punish." With the midterms looming, the Justice Department has taken a series of aggressive steps against Trump's political foes and on issues that he and his allies have focused on for years. Two weeks ago, federal authorities searched the D.C. home of Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar (Minnesota) over allegations that the first Somali-American congresswoman lied on immigration paperwork. Attorneys for Omar, who is up for reelection in November, characterized the search as politically motivated, saying the congresswoman is a critic of Trump who Republicans have spurred baseless accusations against her for years. Blanche and the Justice Department defended the search and its timing. They said the agency's 60-day policy - the unwritten guideline stating that the Justice Department should refrain from taking public law enforcement actions in the two months before an election - is an informal practice and not a written rule. And they have said this policy does not require law enforcement to stop ongoing work during the election season. "We don't do political paybacks," Blanche said at a news conference last week. The week after searching Omar's home, the Justice Department indicted Virginia state Sen. L. Louise Lucas, one of the most powerful Democrats in the commonwealth, as part of a long-running corruption investigation involving a family-run marijuana business. Her attorney said Lucas denied the charges. Blanche and FBI Director Kash Patel appeared together in a rare news conference announcing the charges against the state senator. Lucas, an outspoken Trump critic, and Democrats said the case was politically motivated. Blanche defended the indictment. "What we're doing is very consistent with past practices," Blanche said at the news conference announcing the charges. "People can criticize all they want." The investigation into Lucas was launched during the Biden administration. Lucas's daughter, Lisa Lucas-Burke, was also charged and is on the ballot in November for a Portsmouth City Council seat. The next day, the Justice Department charged two former FBI officials with making false statements to Congress that allegedly hindered a Republican-led House committee as it was investigating President Joe Biden's son Hunter in the lead-up to the 2024 presidential election. Through their attorneys, both ex-officials denied wrongdoing. Those FBI officials had been the subject of right-wing online excoriations for years, with conservatives claiming that they purposely tried to stymie Republican lawmakers investigations into the laptop. The flurry of legal activity continued that evening, with the Justice Department filing an extraordinary lawsuit in Alaska that asked a judge to bar the state from certifying its Senate race results should the Republican incumbent, Dan Sullivan, lose by a margin less than the number of votes received by a similarly named challenger, Dan J. Sullivan. Under that scenario, the department said, the court should investigate whether the result was tainted by voter confusion. Alaska's Republican-led state government seeks to have the lawsuit thrown out. In a remarkable admission highlighting the closeness between Blanche and Trump, the president said he directed the Justice Department to sue Alaska. "I'm the one that said do it," Trump said ahead of a campaign rally in Florida. Blanche has since said the Justice Department has been eyeing the issue for months and came to its own conclusion to file suit. On Monday, the Justice Department's actions hit a crescendo when court documents were unsealed revealing that prosecutors had charged Comey for a third time earlier this month. This time, the Justice Department alleged that he leaked sensitive government material to the media in 2016 while FBI director. Trump fired Comey in 2017 during his first administration. In an extremely rare move, prosecutors did not obtain an indictment through a grand jury to charge Comey, but rather charged him in D.C. with a criminal information. The Justice Department said that it filed it through a criminal information to avoid having the 10-year statute of limitations for the crime take effect. That statute of limitations was set to expire the day prosecutors charged Comey. But critics said that questionable maneuver highlighted the Justice Department's furious attempts to quickly push through what they viewed as a weak case without going through a grand jury, which could have voted not to indict the case. The Justice Department will eventually need to secure an indictment through a grand jury. A Justice Department spokesperson noted that federal officials filed the information under seal on Oct. 5 and that a judge decided to make it public earlier this week at the request of Comey's lawyers. Former Justice Department attorneys questioned the merits of the case. Prosecutors allege that Comey directed his staff in 2016 to talk to a reporter to address what he viewed as misinformation in an article about email surveillance published by another news outlet the previous day. "My reaction to the information is that it's dead on arrival," said Michael Bromwich, a former Justice Department inspector general who is representing defendants being investigated by the Trump administration. "It is remarkable to me that they have brought three terrible cases against the same man." Comey has denied the latest allegations and vowed to fight the case against him. item.title: Israelis await final election results as Netanyahu remains far from defeated
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
JERUSALEM (AP) — Anxious Israelis watched election results near completion Wednesday after the highest voter turnout in over a quarter-century, as no clear winner emerged and weeks of negotiating could lie ahead for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and an array of opposition parties trying to unseat him. Arab-led parties made a historic showing, but it’s not clear if other opponents of Netanyahu's far-right government would form a coalition with them for a majority of seats in parliament. Issues around the Palestinians and their descendants remain incredibly sensitive in Israel. Netanyahu seeks to remain the country's longest-serving prime minister. In defiant comments after the vote — which showed his Likud party losing ground since the 2022 election — he dismissed as treasonous the idea of partnering with Arab parties. On Wednesday, Netanyahu warned against a “dangerous government” that might include them. He won’t work with the Arab-led parties, whose constituents make up 20% of Israel's population, and they have also ruled out any partnership with him. His top challenger, centrist former military chief Gadi Eisenkot , has left the door open to partnering with Arab parties under certain conditions, including their recognition of Israel as a Jewish state and of Hamas as an extremist group. But it's not clear whether some of Eisenkot's likely partners who have ruled out such an alliance will change their minds to force Netanyahu from office. Israeli voters choose parties, not individuals. With 85% of votes counted, Netanyahu’s Likud party has 20.8% and Eisenkot's Yashar party has 16.1%. The official count does not indicate how many seats each will have in parliament, the 120-seat Knesset. Emerging results indicated that neither Netanyahu's nor Eisenkot's coalition blocs would reach the 61 seats needed for a majority; local media projected 53 seats for Likud and allied parties, 48 for Yashar and allied parties and 19 for Arab-led parties. Netanyahu faces a setback but not outright defeat Nearly 78% of eligible voters turned out, the highest since 1999. Final results are expected by the end of the week, and will capture about a half-million absentee ballots yet to be counted from military personnel and diplomats. Voting reflected unease over Netanyahu's alliance with the far-right and anger in a war-weary nation over military draft exemptions for the significant ultra-Orthodox Jewish population; the Likud party's share of the vote declined from 23.4% in 2022. But results suggest opponents were unable to capitalize on the grief caused by the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attack to decisively push him from office. One far-right partner losing support was national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir . For many Israelis, he represented the worst strain of Netanyahu’s government, openly taunting Palestinian detainees and asserting that many in Gaza are “not even people.” Vote-counting suggested Likud would remain the largest party and best placed to be tapped to form a government by Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog. The president, however, isn't required to task the leader of the party holding the most seats. “We must do everything we can, certainly after yesterday, to avoid another round of elections,” Herzog said Wednesday. The most obvious path to a parliamentary majority could involve Eisenkot partnering with Arab-led parties — which have 14.9% of the votes counted — but that's politically challenging. In a speech early Wednesday that focused on national unity, Eisenkot pledged to form a government and promised “a new era — an era of hope." If no one can put together a majority coalition, new elections could be held early next year. Israel held five elections between April 2019 and November 2022 because of a similar stalemate. It is unclear whether thousands of Israelis living abroad would again fly back home to vote , and whether Arab voters would again surge to the polls. Minority governments also are possible, but they must rely on cooperation from parties outside the government to pass legislation. Arab-led parties could hold the key Confronted with Arab parties’ strong election showing, Israelis have renewed a debate about identity. “We have no future here if we do not stop being afraid," said Yair Golan, whose Democrats party supports bringing Arab-led parties into a coalition. "We must no longer accept Netanyahu’s racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes.” Israel’s Arab citizens are descendants of Palestinians who remained in the state after its creation in 1948. They often face discrimination and are viewed with wariness because of their solidarity with the Palestinian cause. That suspicion intensified after Oct. 7, even though Arab citizens were also among those killed and abducted . The mood was joyful overnight at the headquarters of the United Arab List, the lone Arab party to ever join a governing coalition, briefly, in 2021. “We are here, we are not on the sidelines,” party leader Mansour Abbas declared. Some Israelis found that an unusual, if not uncomfortable, prospect. “We are little by little coming to a situation where we have to face reality," said Hanna Doukhan, a voter in Tel Aviv. "I don’t see a possibility to form a government without the Arabs.” Others were hopeful. “This would open the door to repairing our society" while preserving Israel as the national home of the Jewish people, said Eti Wissotzky-Cohen in Tel Aviv. And in Nazareth, one of Israel’s largest Arab cities, Awni Zoabi thanked God for a possible return to rationality in a country where extreme rhetoric has increased . “The Arabic language has become as if it were a crime," Zoabi said. Attitudes over Netanyahu will shape the days ahead Netanyahu has had a nearly unbroken 17-year rule. Israelis were divided over him even before the deadliest attack in the country’s history. The resulting wars , along with settler violence in the occupied West Bank, have stoked worldwide outrage , straining ties with Israel’s closest allies and fueling a rise in antisemitism. Netanyahu’s supporters believe he is protecting Israel’s security and Jewish identity in the face of international pressure and liberal elites at home. “I prefer that (Netanyahu) assembles the coalition,” said Ran Cohen, a Jerusalem resident. “He’s the only one who knows how to do the job properly, knows how to speak to the world.” Detractors say Netanyahu, facing an ongoing corruption trial , dragged out the war in Gaza and its hostage crisis for political reasons. They say he is undermining Israel’s independent judiciary. And they accuse his government of allowing ultra-Orthodox religious Jews to avoid military conscription . Eisenkot is viewed by supporters as a capable leader with sterling security credentials. His son and two nephews were killed in Gaza, and his backers believe that he feels deeply the country's pain. Parties that likely would partner with him have vowed to improve Israel’s international standing and work to conscript ultra-Orthodox men while bolstering the independence of the judiciary. ___ Associated Press writers across Israel contributed to this report. This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/israelis-await-final-election-results-060934179.html

item.title: Classified material missing from Epstein files, documents suggest
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Attorney General Todd Blanche has long maintained that the so-called Epstein files, even those kept from the public, contain no secret information related to national security. When the document releases began last winter, Blanche noted that the Epstein Files Transparency Act authorized withholding information in the interest of national security or foreign policy, but said, "no files are being withheld or redacted on that basis." "There's not some tranche of super-secret documents about Jeffrey Epstein that we're withholding, we're actually not withholding anything based upon [national defense information]," said Blanche, who was deputy attorney general at the time. But the contents of at least three documents in the massive tranche of files indicate classified information was included in files collected by the DOJ. One of the documents shows Blanche's Office of the Deputy Attorney General itself received classified material related to Epstein in March 2025. By law, material can only be classified for national security purposes. What exactly was classified and why remains a mystery. The Department of Justice says it collected 6 million pages of material and ultimately released over 3 million of those pages after reviewing for duplication, attorney-client privilege and relevance to Jeffrey Epstein. Congressional challenges and a lawsuit are casting doubts on the DOJ's claims and demanding the release of more documents that were held back. Clues about classified material Included among the Epstein files is an eight-page timeline of the FBI's New York office's initial efforts last year to track down and deliver its voluminous files to the Justice Department's Washington headquarters. On March 25, 2025, one document shows delivery of "16 Epstein items to ODAG," referring to the Office of the Deputy Attorney General. Among them, items No. 2 and No. 6 are described as "Epstein Transparency Project - Classified Material" and "CDs with classified materials (x2)." The Epstein Transparency Project refers to the Justice Department's effort to review the files and redact , withhold or clear them for release. It is not clear what exactly was identified as classified. Each CD was likely capable of holding hundreds of megabytes of material. Also in the files is an email sent that same day from the unit chief of the National Security Classification Operations Unit — an office whose role is to review FBI documents for classification or declassification. The email includes an attachment labeled "Epstein - Classified Document Memo.docx." The body of the email says there were three documents "identified that remain classified." One was described as an "FBI document which is classified when see-through." A redaction obscures the unit chief's description of the other two documents. The identity of the email's recipient is also redacted. It's also not clear whether the two documents — the email and the list — are referring to the same classified material. Coding system reveals missing pages A CBS News analysis of a numerical coding system used by the DOJ to organize the Epstein files offers clues about some of the documents the department has withheld. The codes don't reveal what's missing, but they do show where gaps exist, raising questions about the DOJ's explanation for why documents were withheld. Among the missing documents are pages from Epstein's own financial records collected as evidence in a federal prosecution. Here's how it works: Documents from the Epstein files are labeled with a string of numbers beginning with the letters EFTA stamped on the bottom right-hand corner; EFTA stands for Epstein Files Transparency Act. Those are called Bates numbers — a common way of organizing massive document batches in legal cases. Every page receives its own number. In the Epstein files, the sequence goes from 1 to 2,858,498, which is the tally of approximately how many pages of documents were released. According to the DOJ, other documents — including court records and investigative files they've previously released — bring the total to over 3 million. Alongside the Epstein files' Bates numbers are other, older coding numbers that appear on many documents. This indicates that those documents had previously been used in federal legal cases, potentially collected as part of an earlier subpoena. For instance, Bates coding on some of the documents is from the Ghislaine Maxwell criminal case and was used to organize files given to Maxwell's legal team ahead of her 2021 trial as part of the discovery process. Other Bates numbers indicate documents were collected from Epstein's banks, including JPMorgan and Deutsche Bank, during the FBI's investigation into his trafficking activities. Similar gap analyses have been done in the past by independent researchers. Missing financial documents Finding gaps in these documents is a simple process of counting. In tens of thousands of instances, the main EFTA number will advance by one but the other Bates numbers advance by two or more. Those gaps indicate pages that had been there before were likely removed at some point after the DOJ obtained them. Take the images below: The EFTA number advances by one but the JPM-SDNY and SDNY_GM numbers advance by 2, as do the page numbers from the original document. In another example, a series of around 4,500 images of checks from Epstein's accounts has gaps where 66 of those check images should be. Oftentimes the missing image is only the front or the back of the check, although in several cases both are missing. Comparing all of these numbers against the final EFTA page numbers, it is possible to calculate that there are tens of thousands of pages of documents that are missing from these sections, with no clear reason why. "Financial records were not a permissible category for removal," Barbara McQuade, the former U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District of Michigan, told CBS News. Like every federal prosecutor, she says she is very familiar with Bates numbers. "It's the reason you have Bates numbers, so you notice something like that," she said. The DOJ hasn't responded to CBS News' recent inquiries about the Epstein files, but it has previously said that every document required to be released by the Epstein Files Transparency Act has been released, and the remaining files were unrelated, privileged, or were duplicative. Email gaps Another sequence of Bates numbers that provide a map to where documents were removed appears to be from a preliminary processing of the files. One large sequence of those have "R1" in between EFTA and the page number. This R1 numbering is found across approximately 995,000 released pages, between p. 61 and p. 2,214,171 in the files. Each page is also labeled with an EFTA page number. While the EFTAs are sequential, the R1s have gaps which range from 1 page to hundreds of pages. Each time a gap appears — for example, if the EFTA advances by 1 but the R1 advances by 2 — it's evidence that pages were removed. By comparing these sequences it's possible to identify gaps where documents, mostly emails, were removed between that earlier review and the final release. No partial emails turned up in the thousands of documents we examined, so the removals appear to be entire email exchanges. Here's what a section of that looks like: The emails are not sequential in date and jump by days, months and years, so knowing what was removed from context is simply not possible. But the results of calculating the differences between the first and last of the numbers in this earlier sequence versus the later sequence is 1.2 million pages, which is the total number of identified gaps from just this one section. Most of the documents in this section are emails to or from Jeffrey Epstein, including communication with young women who would later accuse him of abuse; email exchanges with his business associates; messages to or from his assistant, Lesley Groff; or emails sent or received by Ghislaine Maxwell. "De-duping" There is one possible explanation for many of the email gaps. Instructions given to DOJ attorneys working on processing the redactions state: "If the document is an email chain and the most-inclusive email (i.e., containing all the back-and-forth) has already been reviewed and redacted as appropriate for production, the interstitial back-and-forth can be marked as duplicates." In other words, all emails exchanged prior to the last email in a chain can be considered a duplicate, because the last one should include all of the messages, and eliminating the duplicates will speed up the redaction process. Once a document is marked as a duplicate, it would likely be excluded from the files. If that was the case, this was only partially accomplished because duplicate emails still exist throughout the files. There's also the possibility that errors in the process could have resulted in crucial emails mistakenly being deleted. Lack of transparency The review and redaction process was conducted by hundreds of DOJ attorneys working under a compressed timeline. Given the scale of the task, it's possible that pages were withheld as a result of honest mistakes. But without a roadmap to the redactions and removals, it's impossible to make that determination. Independent journalist Katie Phang is suing the Justice Department, seeking the release of more files as well as an explanation of redactions and removals. A federal judge has made several rulings in her favor and the DOJ is appealing those rulings. As part of her lawsuit, Phang is asking the court to appoint a special master to review the files. "If it wasn't intentional, then was it gross negligence? Were you just lazy? If it was intentional then I think there's [expletive] there that they don't want people to see," Phang told CBS News. "My speculation runs an entire spectrum of reaction — but at the end of the day it just makes the DOJ look bad." The DOJ has acknowledged making several mistakes. It admitted to removing, and then restoring, a photo of now Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on a 2012 visit to Epstein's island , contradicting claims Lutnick had previously made about his contacts with Epstein . Last year, DOJ officials claimed a minute was missing from prison security video from the night Epstein died, which turned out to not be true . "This is a case where the process has inhibited public trust in what is ultimately released, and there's a long tradition of this, whether it's the Pentagon Papers or the Epstein files," said attorney Stanley Brand, a veteran litigator and distinguished fellow in law and government at Penn State Dickinson Law. "This is just another piece where the government process, where making this stuff available just fuels suspicion that there's something we're not seeing, and I don't know that ever gets resolved." item.title: Democrats have a big early voting lead, but another trend may matter more
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
People wait in line to participate in early voting for the midterm elections in Cary, North Carolina, on October 25, 2026. —Allison Joyce—AFP/Getty Images Election Day is still a week away. But with early voting for the midterms underway in nearly every state, tens of millions of Americans have already cast their ballots , offering an initial glimpse into how the pivotal elections may play out. As of Tuesday afternoon, nearly 33 million people have voted since early voting windows opened in some states over a month ago, according to tracking by the University of Florida’s Election Lab. Around half of those votes have been cast in person, while the other half were submitted by mail. With days of early voting left to go before Election Day on Nov. 3, that figure already represents more than a quarter of the roughly 122 million Americans who voted in the 2022 midterms. Michael McDonald, a political science professor at the University of Florida who runs the Election Lab, stresses to TIME that early voting data cannot in and of itself be relied on to predict the outcome of the elections. But he says it can reveal other informative aspects of voting behavior. “Once you start seeing consistency across multiple days of voting and across multiple states, it starts giving us more confidence that whatever we're seeing in terms of relative engagement, that's likely going to carry through to election day,” McDonald says. Here are some of the notable trends emerging in the early voting data as Election Day nears. Democrats are outpacing Republicans in early ballots Registered Democrats so far represent a larger share of early voters in the midterms than Republicans, having cast roughly 45% of early ballots compared to 31% cast by GOP voters, according to the University of Florida’s Election Lab data. Another 24% of Americans who have voted early are not registered with either party. This data is only available for the 27 states that have a formal party registration system, and signifies only the party with which a voter is registered, not the candidates selected on their ballot. Experts caution that Democrats’ higher turnout in the early vote does not guarantee they’ll maintain that edge, with tens of millions more Americans still expected to show up at the polls. Republicans are anticipated to make up ground on Election Day, as they have in recent years. A Pew Research survey conducted following the 2024 elections showed that nearly 40% of registered Republican voters cast their ballot in person on Election Day, compared to 28% of registered Democratic voters. “We expect the Democrats to build up a lead in the early vote, and Election Day tends to be a Republican day, so you can't just look at the early vote as it is now,” McDonald tells TIME. Polling has shown, however, that Democratic engagement and enthusiasm is higher than it is for Republicans in the lead-up to the elections. According to a PBS News /NPR/Marist poll released on Tuesday, 52% of likely voters said they would back the Democratic candidate in their House district, while 44% would back the Republican candidate. Independent likely voters favored Democratic candidates by 13 points. More Democrats than Republicans also said in the survey they were very enthusiastic about voting, at 71% and 61% respectively. Another poll from the Pew Research Center earlier this month similarly showed greater engagement and stated motivation from voters backing Democrats: 78% of voters who voiced support for the Democratic candidate in their House district said who controls Congress “really matters,” compared to 69% of voters who backed Republican candidates who said the same. Such polls have suggested a “blue wave” of Democratic support might determine the midterms, but Republicans have pushed back against the numbers. Read More: Polls Point to a Blue Wave. Here's Why Republicans Say They're Wrong Bernard Fraga, a political science professor at Emory University, tells TIME that the relative lack of Republican enthusiasm in polls and trailing GOP turnout in early voting shows that support within the party, and for President Donald Trump, has waned. “This is a story about Democrats who voted in 2024 persisting, and Republicans who voted in 2024 so far at least staying home,” he says. The midterms come as Trump’s approval rating has hit near record lows amid widespread dissatisfaction with his handling of the war in Iran and the economy. A Reuters/Ipsos poll released on Monday put Trump’s approval rating at 32%, up one percentage point from last week, when the same poll recorded the lowest approval rating of his second term. Fraga says that Republicans are frustrated with what he describes as “failures” of the Trump Administration, which he asserts have decreased GOP voters’ support for their party and led them to stay home rather than casting ballots early. “Even for steadfast Republican voters, they look at the state of the economy, for example, and say that they're not too enthusiastic about voting,” he says. “Reading the trends, it's clear that Democrats are enthusiastic and mobilized to a much greater degree than even the Republican voters.” Simon Rosenberg, a long-time Democratic strategist, contends that independents are also more likely to be voting in favor of Democrats, given recent polling , which has shown that more independent likely voters support Democratic candidates. One YouGov poll found that 54% of independents said they’d vote for Democratic candidates, versus 27% who said they’d vote for Republican candidates. Another PBS/NPR/Marist poll showed that independents favored Democrats by a margin of 25 points. Given such polling, Rosenberg believes that the number of people voting for Democratic candidates is actually higher than the partisan breakdown in early voting data explicitly indicates. Hispanic voters are turning out early in higher numbers than other recent elections Rosenberg says that the most significant data coming out of early voting is the number of Hispanic people voting early. So far, Hispanic early voting participation is outpacing its levels at the same point in the election cycle in 2022 and 2024. Presidential election years such as 2024 typically yield higher voter turnout, which Rosenberg says makes the 2026 figures to date all the more notable and surprising. “It's almost certain that this heightened performance will carry over through Election Day, and that this will become one of the big storylines of the election,” he says. “It's a universal trend that we're seeing all across the country.” This trend is most noticeable in states with high Hispanic populations, like Texas. In one of the most closely watched—and expensive —Senate races this year, James Talarico is vying to become the first Democrat elected to the Senate from Texas since 1988 in a tightly contested battle against the state’s Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton. Over 4 million votes have been cast early, or an estimated 41% of the total votes expected in the race, according to tracking by VoteHub . As of Monday, Talarico was forecast to hold a narrow two-point lead in the early vote. The state's Hispanic population, one of the highest in the U.S. per capita, represents 24% of the vote as of Monday, according to VoteHub, a percentage point higher than the share it made up in the final vote tally in the 2024 election. Another analysis reported by The Texas Tribune showed that the Hispanic early vote in Texas has already surpassed the early vote numbers from 2024 and 2022. “What we can see here is just eye-popping numbers for Hispanics,” McDonald said about the group’s early voter turnout not only in Texas, but around the U.S. “If Hispanics are showing up in force now, it's almost with certainty going to change the overall … diversity of the electorate in this election cycle.” As a result, McDonald contends that “we're going to see larger swings to the Democrats in more diverse states.” Polling has indicated that Hispanic and Latino voters, a demographic that helped propel Trump back to the White House two years ago, widely disapprove of the President and the Republican Party heading into midterms. Sixty-six percent of Latino voters surveyed in late September by an NBC News/Telemundo poll said that Trump’s deportation policies have gone too far, while 75% disapprove of his handling of the economy and the cost of living. The poll also found that more Latino voters hold a negative view of the GOP than at any point since 2016. Another Reuters/Ipsos poll released on Oct. 5 showed that just 24% of Hispanic Americans approved of Trump’s performance in the White House, the lowest such rating the President has received across both of his presidential terms. And just 52% of Hispanic voters who responded to the poll planned to vote Democratic, double the level of support for Republicans among the demographic. How predictive is early voting data? Rosenberg cautions that early voting “can tell you a lot, but it can't tell you everything,” and that voter turnout can shift from day to day. He notes that early voting returns showed Kamala Harris leading in the 2024 presidential election, and that she still lost after a strong gain in Republican turnout for Trump. But he contends that “the lack of intensity that we're seeing in many rural and Republican counties around the country does not bode well for them for Election Day.” Fraga says that in general, political scientists are skeptical of using early voting data to predict election outcomes. This has been especially true, he notes, in the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic, which saw Democrats cast early votes by mail at a significantly higher rate than Republicans, who were more likely to vote early at polls, a dynamic that made it harder to draw on the early vote to confidently predict outcomes on Election Day. Now, though, “the partisan distribution of voters has become somewhat more stable,” he says. “So we can use that information to now have a better comparison, and as a result, early voting data sheds a lot more light on what's likely to happen in November.” “It's not determinative. It's not going to predict what's going to happen,” Rosenberg says. “But every campaign in the country right now is living and dying on this early vote data.” Richard Hall contributed reporting. item.title: Defeated Brazilian presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro and family land in Miami
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
MIAMI (AP) — Defeated Brazilian presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro and his family arrived in Miami on Wednesday, after he refused to concede to President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva then fled the country. In a circuitous journey, Bolsonaro left for Argentina on Tuesday with his wife and two daughters, then traveled to Ecuador, according to Argentina officials and flight data. The 45-year-old senator and his family arrived in Florida a day after the Trump administration granted them United States visas . Bolsonaro, an ally of U.S. President Donald Trump, visited the White House in May. Bolsonaro’s father, Jair Bolsonaro, also fled to Florida after losing the 2022 presidential election to Lula before returning to Brazil three months later. Flávio Bolsonaro is under investigation by Brazil’s Supreme Court, accused of corruption, money laundering and tax evasion. The court had ordered him to hand over his regular and diplomatic passports by noon Tuesday. It remained unclear whether he had complied, but allies said late Tuesday he also has an Italian passport. Bolsonaro lands in Miami Argentina's migration authority said Bolsonaro, his wife Fernanda Antunes Figueira Bolsonaro, and his daughters Carolina Figueira Bolsonaro and Luiza Figueira Bolsonaro crossed into the country at 10:50 p.m. Tuesday. They entered via the Tancredo Neves International Bridge, a primary border checkpoint linking Brazil to Argentina’s northeastern province of Misiones. “Those who did so possessed valid travel documentation and faced no legal impediments to entering the country,” the Argentine migration authority said on X. The four boarded a private charter flight operated by aviation company Baires Fly S.A. at 11:30 p.m. local time, the authority said. According to the filed flight plan, the aircraft departed for Guayaquil, Ecuador. His route via Argentina is almost certain to cause a diplomatic rift between Lula and Argentine President Javier Milei, a Trump ally who traveled to Brazil to take part in Bolsonaro’s campaign. Flight tracking website FlightRadar24 showed a plane fitting the description of Bolsonaro’s landed in Guayaquil at about 4 a.m. local time, then took off minutes later for Miami-Opa locka Executive Airport. The plane carrying Bolsonaro and his family landed in Miami at around 9:30 a.m. EDT. Before they landed in Florida, Lula, who turned 81 on Tuesday, told dozens of supporters outside the presidential residence in Brasilia that he didn't have precise information about Bolsonaro’s whereabouts, but said he had left Brazil. “I regret that he left Brazil, because he could have stayed here and proven that the accusations are not true,” Lula said. “This act of leaving Brazil is shameful.” Paulo Figueiredo, a close Bolsonaro ally who lives in the U.S., said in a short statement he couldn't confirm information from foreign authorities, but that “Flávio Bolsonaro is well, in security and resting with his family.” Figueiredo said there would be a press conference Thursday in Miami to discuss the case. Representatives of Brazil's government didn't immediately respond to requests for comment from The Associated Press. Trump rejects Brazilian election results Trump said early Wednesday that he would approve of Bolsonaro coming to the U.S., calling him and his family “fine people.” “The election was really strange, and I thought it was terrible,” Trump told reporters at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, after returning from campaigning in Texas on Tuesday. He did not elaborate, but stressed that he didn't endorse the election results. Leaders all over the world and the Organization of American States endorsed the result and congratulated Lula, who was reelected by a margin of about 4.4 million votes in the second and final round. On Tuesday, Milei's administration spokesman Adrián Ravier said “there is no asylum request (from Bolsonaro) and there is nothing more to add.” Bolsonaro visited his father, who is under house arrest, before leaving Brazil The defeated candidate was served with a Supreme Court order to surrender his Brazilian passports Monday. In a video, he said he received it outside the home where his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, is serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest for attempting a coup following his 2022 election loss to Lula. A Brazilian diplomat who was not authorized to speak about the matter publicly told The Associated Press that Bolsonaro used an Italian passport to enter Argentina and did not leave records in Brazilian check points, as they are not required to exit. The diplomat said Brazil’s federal police were not monitoring Bolsonaro when he left his home in Brasilia as he did not have any warrant for arrest from the Supreme Court. Flávio Bolsonaro said in a video Monday that he was attempting to organize opposition to the election results among his congressional colleagues. His eight-year term as a senator expires Jan. 31, 2027. Brazil's Supreme Court is investigating Bolsonaro for allegedly using a sports betting company to launder fraudulent deductions from government pensions paid to senior citizens. In a separate case, he is accused of accepting millions of dollars from a disgraced banker . ___ Mauricio Savarese reported from Sao Paulo. ___ Follow AP’s coverage of Latin America and the Caribbean at https://apnews.com/hub/latin-america This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/articles/fl-vio-bolsonaro-flees-brazil-090538347.html

But state officials and other legal advocates opposing the DOJ lawsuit countered that the litigation violated longstanding Constitutional principles mandating that states have control over their elections -- and could have chaotic consequences for the state in tabulating final vote counts in the weeks ahead. Appeals court declines to step in on Trump administration's California voting case Notably in closing out the hearing, Judge Carter appeared to admonish the administration over its recent letters to state officials around California suggesting it could prosecute them if they are involved in tabulating ballots that could be from the list of alleged likely noncitizens. "This court believes it would be wise that any threats to state and county elected employees cease immediately," Carter said. "Good night." item.title: Trump and Talarico draw competing crowds in an unlikely Texas battleground

President Trump and Texas Senate candidate James Talarico (D) shared their competing visions Tuesday as the two held dueling rallies in the Lone Star State one week before the midterm elections. Trump did two rallies in Texas — the first in Corpus Christi and another in Lubbock . It’s his fourth trip to Texas to support Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton. Talarico held his own rally in Lubbock on Tuesday. He was in Corpus Christi on Saturday. The Texas race is one of the most contested and watched Senate races in the country. Talarico and Paxton remain close in the polls — RealClearPolling calls the race a toss-up, with Talarico holding a slight lead. A Democrat winning the Senate seat would be a shock — a Democrat has not won a U.S. Senate race in Texas since 1988, and Trump won the state by nearly 14 percentage points in the 2024 presidential election. Democrats are vying to take control of the House and the Senate. The party would need to win four seats to win control of the Senate. The president started off his rally in Corpus Christi saying that Texans would defeat “Democrat Communist James Talafreako,” using the nickname he’s given to the candidate. At both rallies, Trump criticized Talarico on a range of issues like immigration, the Second Amendment and barbecue. “If you’re running in Texas and if you don’t like guns, and if you don’t like meat and if you don’t like oil, I think you should be losing by a lot,” Trump said at the first rally about Talarico. “Where the hell did they get this guy?” Trump spoke heavily about a Venezuelan oil tanker that arrived in Texas on Tuesday and is carrying oil to be refined in the state. He said Talarico would try to take it away. “Talafreako stated that he wants to dismantle Texas oil and gas and capitalism itself. He wants to take it apart,” Trump continued, adding that Talarico will “kill millions of Texas jobs.” In Lubbock, Trump said Talarico “wants to get rid of your guns. He wants to get rid of your oil. Wants to get rid of your meat. He can't stand the stuff.” Talarico has denied being vegan and said he supports the Second Amendment, but he advocates for gun control. Talarico, for his part, thanked Texans for showing up for his rally in Lubbock, just 3 miles away from Trump’s, invoking Trump’s nickname for him. “That’s a lot of Talafreakos in one room,” he said. He said Texans are “ready for change” and hit the Trump administration over the Iran war and tariffs. “Change that will roll back these corrupt tariffs that are raising grocery prices. Change that will end this corrupt war in the Middle East, driving up gas prices,” he said. “We are done with the extremism and the corruption. We're done with the politics of division, and we are ready for something new.” The Democratic Texan hit on Paxton, calling him the “most corrupt politician in Texas.” “Ken Paxton is everything that's wrong with our politics,” he said. “He doesn't serve us. He serves himself.” “Ken has spent his entire career enriching himself and his donors. I've spent my career working with both parties to cut your property taxes, lower your housing costs, and capping your insulin copays,” Talarico continued. “I have a legislative record. item.title: The stock market's best 6 months start Monday, with a 76-year streak on the line
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The stock market's favorite season starts Monday. For decades, November through April has beaten the rest of the year by a mile. That's the Halloween indicator , also called the “best six months” or "sell in May." Buy stocks at the end of October, hold them through April, then step aside for the summer. Yale Hirsch found the pattern in 1986. "You can divide the year into two sections and have practically all the gains in one six-month section and very little in the other," his son Jeffrey Hirsch, editor in chief of the Stock Trader's Almanac, wrote in the 2026 edition. Since 1950, the Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI ) has gained an average of about 7% from November through April, versus less than 1% from May through October, according to the Stock Trader's Almanac. Put $10,000 into only the good half each year, and it grew to about $1.3 million. Put it into only the bad half, and it shrank to about $4,300. This has held up since its discovery. In the 39 years after 1986, the good half turned $10,000 into about $1.2 million, versus about $5,800 for the bad half, by the Stock Trader Almanac's count. The 'worst 6 months' aren't so bad anymore By Yahoo Finance calculations, the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) gained an average of about 7% from November through April between 1950 and 1987, versus about 1% from May through October. Yahoo Finance Since 1988, the summer stretch has averaged about 3%. Over the past 10 years, the two halves have been dead even, at about 7% each. May through October came out ahead in five of those years, including a gain of about 23% in 2025. Hirsch has seen the calendar shift too. "Anticipators, shifts in cultural behavior and faster information flow have altered seasonality in recent years," he wrote. Index funds and 401(k)s now keep money flowing into stocks every month — one reason "sell in May" has been a bad strategy this century . This year, the S&P 500 is up about 6% since the end of April. Midterm years are where the good half still shines. In midterm election years since 1950, October and November have been the S&P 500's two best months, according to the Stock Trader’s Almanac. And the November-April stretch after a midterm has risen 19 straight times since 1950, with an average gain of about 15%, by Yahoo Finance calculations. That follows stocks' best stretch of a midterm year , the eight sessions around Election Day. None of this makes summer safe. May through October hold some of the market's worst stretches, including drops of about 15% in 2001, about 18% in 2002, and about 30% in 2008. The better lesson may be to hedge in May rather than go away. The midterm streak goes on the line Monday. If the S&P 500 finishes April 30 above its Oct. 30 close, it will be 20 for 20 since 1950. A loss would be the first after a midterm since 1946. Internal AI tools helped analyze interview transcripts, research, and draft this post. item.title: At least 64 people killed in high-speed train collision in central Spain
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By David Latona, Guillermo Martinez and Michael Francis Gore URDA, Spain, Oct 28 (Reuters) - At least 64 people died when two Spanish high-speed trains collided on Wednesday, with rescue workers scouring the wreckage for more bodies after Spain's second deadly rail accident this year. Hundreds of ambulances, funeral home vans and helicopters were parked next to one of the trains, with several carriages ‌on an elevated section of track while twisted metal, broken panels and wreckage could be seen strewn across an embankment beneath the line where at least three carriages had plunged down. Evacuated passengers ‌streamed along a road near the scene, some splattered with blood or with their wounds bandaged, others wheeling suitcases and being given water by volunteers who said it had been donated from neighbouring towns. Miguel, a passenger travelling with several colleagues in the rear car of ​one of the trains, described to COPE radio the moment of the accident. "We heard a massive roar, a truly enormous thud that went on for 10 seconds, as if the train were about to derail. Through the right-hand window, we could see a wrecked train," he said. OPERATOR RENFE SAYS CIRCUMSTANCES BEING INVESTIGATED The collision comes nine months after an accident between high-speed trains belonging to the same operators and on the same line that killed 46 people. That crash in January, which occurred after a train derailed and smashed into an oncoming train near Adamuz, in Cordoba province, triggered a debate about the level of investment in railway maintenance in recent years. A person briefed on Wednesday's disaster said ‌a train operated by private consortium Iryo stopped near Toledo on orders from ⁠infrastructure manager ADIF due to a signal fault. A train operated by Renfe then struck the stationary train at high speed, causing several carriages of both trains to derail, the person said. Renfe said in a statement that after being authorised to continue its journey, its train had crashed into the Iryo train that had remained stationary "for reasons we ⁠don't know". "The Renfe train continued on its way as instructed, and a collision occurred. The exact sequence of events, the traffic conditions and the circumstances of the impact will have to be established by the investigation," Renfe said. There was no immediate response to a Reuters request for comment from Iryo or Adif. PASSENGER DESCRIBES SEEING FATALITIES Castilla-La Mancha regional government said the death toll had risen to 64. Rescue workers were going carriage by carriage looking for other victims. Authorities gave no immediate figure for ​the ​number of injured but Health Minister Mónica García urged people in a post on X to donate blood. Castilla-La Mancha ​region spokesperson Esther Padilla said 147 people had been travelling on the Iryo train ‌and 397 on the Renfe train. Eduarda, a passenger on the Iryo train, told Cadena SER radio she felt a strong impact that threw her forward, initially making her think the train had made an emergency stop. She only realised the seriousness of the accident after seeing injured people and being told to evacuate. After climbing down an embankment to safety, she saw what she described as a catastrophic scene, with part of the train hanging down the slope and a fire in one carriage. Emergency responders, including a helicopter, police and ambulances, arrived within about 20 minutes, she said. "I saw dead people," she said. The Renfe and Iryo trains crashed just after 9 a.m., causing two Iryo wagons to derail, a spokesperson for the Castilla-La Mancha region said. Renfe said it had activated a special line for families of victims and expressed its condolences. Iryo said it had activated emergency protocols. The causes of ‌the January accident near Cordoba are still under investigation. A preliminary report by Spain's Civil Guard in February pointed to ​defects in the track, rail or weld between two sections of track as the main hypothesis for the accident, but kept seven ​other theories open. ELECTION DUE NEXT MONTH The latest accident comes as Spain gears up for an election ​on November 29. Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez was on his way to the scene of the crash, his office said. The opposition People's Party cancelled all campaign events, a ‌spokesperson said. "Shocked by the serious train accident in Toledo. My affection, solidarity, and support ​to all the victims and their families," Sanchez said ​on X. Accidents, including derailments and collisions, increased from 45 in 2016 to 57 in 2024 and 69 last year, according to Spain's railway safety authority. some 25 million passengers used a high-speed train in Spain in the first half of the year, a decline of roughly 14% compared with the same period last year, according to a Reuters analysis of data from Spain's competition authority. European Commission data shows ​Spain's maintenance investment in its roughly 4,000 km (2,485 miles) of high-speed lines has ‌lagged large European peers, despite an unmatched drive to expand the network. Spain spent an average of about €1.5 billion a year from 2018 to 2022 on its high-speed network, more than any ​other country. However, the vast majority went to new infrastructure with only some 16% earmarked for maintenance, renewal and upgrades. (Reporting by David Latona, Emma Pinedo, Mireia Merino, Corina Pons, Victoria Waldersee, ​Benjamin Mejias, Joan Faus and Pietro Lombardi; Writing by Charlie Devereux; Editing by Toby Chopra and Alison Williams) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/articles/two-high-speed-trains-rear-083828936.html

Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, endorsed Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins for governor Tuesday, passing over three Republican candidates, including President Donald Trump's pick, Bernadette Wilson. "And I'm very grateful that she wanted to step up and be a part of the coalition that we're building." The Republican candidates are Wilson, former Anchorage Mayor Dave Bronson, and former Alaska Attorney General Treg Taylor. Trump endorsed Wilson earlier in October. Wilson dismissed Murkowski's endorsement of Kreiss-Tomkins. "Given that Senator Lisa Murkowski abandoned Alaska values a long time ago, I am not surprised that she has endorsed 'Just Keep Taxing' JKT," Wilson said in a statement. The NBC News Decision Desk rates the gubernatorial race as leaning Democratic, although Trump carried Alaska in the 2016, 2020, and 2024 presidential elections.
